value.overview: The Great Horned Owl (Bubo virginianus) is one of the largest and most widely distributed owls in the Americas. It is recognized by its prominent ear tufts, broad wings, yellow eyes, and deep hooting call. This powerful nocturnal predator occupies habitats ranging from forests and wetlands to savannas, farmland, and urban areas. In Costa Rica it is an uncommon and very localized resident, reported mainly in the Central Valley and other suitable open, wooded landscapes.
value.classification: The Great Horned Owl belongs to the owl family Strigidae and the genus Bubo. It is represented by several regional forms across North, Central, and South America.
value.identification: A large, heavily built owl with conspicuous feathered ear tufts, a broad head, yellow eyes, and a dark-edged facial disk. Plumage is generally brown, gray, and buff, with extensive dark barring and mottling that provides camouflage. The throat often shows a pale or whitish area. Its large, fully feathered feet and powerful talons are characteristic. The deep, resonant hoot is often delivered in repeated phrases, with males and females sometimes calling together.
value.rangeHabitat: The species occurs across much of North and South America, using woodlands, forest edges, savannas, wetlands, agricultural areas, and towns where suitable roosts and nesting sites remain. In Costa Rica it is considered a very rare resident rather than a regular widespread species. Reliable national records are concentrated especially in the Central Valley, including areas near Cartago and Alajuela, with occasional observations elsewhere such as Guanacaste. Suitable Costa Rican habitat includes savannas, pastures, coffee-growing areas, and open country with scattered trees, hedgerows, or forest patches.
value.migrationStatus: Generally resident and sedentary, although young birds disperse after leaving the nest. In Costa Rica, the species is reported as a very rare resident; there is no reliable evidence that it is a regular passage migrant or seasonal visitor there.
value.breeding: Great Horned Owls usually nest in trees, but they commonly reuse abandoned nests made by other large birds and may also nest on cliffs, buildings, or other elevated structures. They defend a territory and begin courtship with hooting and other displays. The female usually lays a small clutch of white eggs and incubates them while the male provides food. Young remain dependent for several weeks after fledging. Detailed information on breeding in Costa Rica is limited, and confirmed national nesting data are scarce.
value.dietFeeding: This owl is an opportunistic predator that takes a broad range of prey. Mammals such as rodents, rabbits, opossums, and squirrels are important, but it also captures birds, reptiles, amphibians, and large insects when available. It hunts mainly from a perch at night, scanning open ground and woodland edges before making a silent attack. Its strong talons allow it to kill relatively large prey, which it may carry or consume at the capture site.
value.behavior: The Great Horned Owl is primarily nocturnal and usually roosts quietly during the day in dense foliage, cavities, or shaded structures. It is territorial and may advertise its presence with deep hoots, especially during courtship and breeding. Flight is powerful but quiet because of the owl's specialized wing feathers. Individuals can adapt to human-dominated landscapes when nesting trees, safe roosts, and adequate prey are available. In Costa Rica, its rarity and secretive habits make encounters uncommon.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered broadly stable, although local populations may fluctuate and regional monitoring is uneven. In Costa Rica, it is very rare and localized, so its national abundance and trend are not well quantified.
